Aside from solar and radioisotope power, is there anything else that can be used to power those electric systems of spacecraft?

Spacecraft commonly rely on their carried fuel as a source of electric power, combining hydrogen and oxygen within a fuel cell to produce power and water. There are many possible variations on this, based on different 'redox' solutions/compounds that might be carried as cargo or be part of a rocket fuel. Hydrogen isn't so compressible, even in cryogenic liquid form, and tends to leak through containers so it's often more efficient to 'package' it. One form for that is as a 'hydride' such as solid sodium hydride. Hydrides are very volatile and dangerous in large volumes, which is why we never used them to power vehicles, but if you package it in small amounts it's relatively safe. So you could break open small capsules of hydride in water and they would react to produce hydrogen and hydroxide (lye in the case of sodium hydroxide) which you then feed into a fuel cell to produce power and more water. This was once the basis of a commercial product called Power Balls that was intended to power automobiles and small fuel appliances. It made hydride vastly safer than gasoline and clean and non-toxic enough that you could sell it in a grocery store. Another more exotic hydride is liquid borohydride which only reacts to release hydrogen in the presence of a metal catalyst, allowing you to finely control the hydrogen release by limiting the flow of the liquid.

Some redox solutions are recyclable complimentary pairs, allowing them to function as a reusable battery whose capacity is determined by how much liquid you carry. For instance, a solution of vanadium in sulphuric acid. If you put two isolated tanks of this solution through a fuel cell while supplying electric power, it polarizes the solutions and stores the electric energy. Then you can run the solutions through the fuel cell again to take the power out. This can be done simultaneously and at different voltages/currents using different fuel cells, or parts of the same fuel cell stack, in line with the storage tanks. So it makes for a good way to combine diverse sources of renewable energy and different simultaneous levels of output power. The catch is that all your hardware has to be made of plastic or ceramic to cope with the acidic solution. Vanadium redox is already used for data center power backup and buffer energy storage for wind turbines.

Spacecraft can also burn fuels to run engines or turbines to generate power much as we conventionally do on Earth. They can also produce power from combustible fuels more directly with things like infrared photovoltaics--which is like a solar photovoltaic panel that uses infrared light radiated from a heat source rather than visible light. Such systems currently exist and have been used as a solid-state alternative to motor generators and for co-generation of electric power from small wood/pellet stoves and building heating furnaces.

Various forms of nuclear reactors beyond thermal radioisotope nuclear batteries are possible. All the sorts of nuclear power we use today have been explored for space use, but their large shielding requirements and the fear of spreading radioactive materials across large portions of the Earth in the even of a launch accident have hampered their development. Even using relatively safe nuclear batteries in very small systems remains highly controversial and there has been periodic public hysteria about this.

Conventional chemical batteries and super-capacitors are commonly used on spacecraft but, of course, have the common limitations we're familiar with. In science fiction we sometimes hear of another kind of speculative super-battery called a nuclear isomer battery. A nuclear isomer is a 'metastable' radioisotope that can be switched or pumped between a very long half-life state and a very short half-life state by another source of energy, like a laser. Such nuclear isomers do exist and are used in nuclear medicine, but only have modest decay rates. In a conventional radioisotope nuclear battery, the energy output is always 'on' because the radioisotope--usually a form of plutonium--is constantly emitting with a relatively short but modest decay rate. With a nuclear isomer battery you could turn this decay on and off and have a very short decay, releasing a huge amount of energy instantaneously. It would be like having a small nuclear bomb whose energy is very directed and that you could switch on and off. Thus DARPA has supposedly done research into these as a kind of nuclear weapon that would circumvent nuclear proliferation treaties, because the isomer material wouldn't be considered a normal fissionable material. Unfortunately--or fortunately, depending on how you look at it--this idea remains science fiction as we have yet to create/discover a metastable isomer that can work this well.

Laser driven lightsail spacecraft, like the recently proposed Starshot concept, would use the same laser energy propelling the spacecraft as as source of energy for electric power using photovoltaics tailored to the laser's spectrum.

Another interesting way for spacecraft to generate electric power is by tapping the Earth itself as a dynamo. This is the principle behind the concept of electrodynamic tether systems. There has been some experiment with the use of tethers as a limited means of spacecraft propulsion through momentum transfer. But because the Earth has a magnetic field, an orbiting spacecraft is rather like the rotor in a dynamo. So if a tether is conductive, it can induce an electrical potential relative to its length. There's a lot of potential power to tap this way--some experiments having failed because the power generated overloaded and burned the tether. Electrodynamic tethers can also function as a kind of solar sail, exploiting the electromagnetic force produced by the plasma solar wind. It is said this can also be used in interstellar travel by tapping the electrodynamic potential of the interstellar medium as a vehicle is traveling at very high velocities, the compromise being a very small cost in velocity as the spacecraft creates its own electromagnetic drag.
